Customer service: 54% still prefer the phone

Chat, messaging apps, social media, automated assistants: contact channels have multiplied. You might think the phone has lost its place. The data says the opposite.

According to a 2022 survey in Statista's dossier on customer service in the US, 54% of respondents preferred phone calls to resolve a problem with customer service. The phone remains the preferred channel, and yet it is the one companies analyze least.

Several surveys, the same finding

The 2022 figure is not an isolated one. In a 2020 survey, 43% of US customers said they preferred voice channels to interact with customer service, nine points more than in 2018. Back in 2017, 51% saw the phone as the channel offering the fastest resolution.

These surveys do not ask exactly the same question and come from different years, so they should not be compared point by point. But they all point in the same direction: when a problem matters, many customers prefer to talk to someone.

The phone keeps an advantage other channels struggle to match: the ability to explain a complex situation in real time and get a tailored answer.

Phone also suits the moments when customers are stressed or worried, such as a blocked account or a missed delivery.

Preferences vary by generation

Statista's dossier on call centers in the US states that in 2024, almost all baby boomers preferred live phone conversations to contact customer service. For Gen Z, Gen X and millennials, the most popular channel was email.

Companies therefore deal with customers who have different habits. Older customers, often loyal and high-value, favor calling. Younger ones write more, but they also turn to the phone when the stakes are high or when writing has not worked.

Dropping or degrading the phone channel means risking poor service for a valuable part of the customer base.

It also means that the phone remains the channel where loyal, long-standing customers express their dissatisfaction. Missing what they say is missing an early warning on some of the most valuable relationships.

The richest channel, the least used

A call contains a considerable amount of information: the exact reason for contact, the words the customer chooses, their tone, their level of irritation or satisfaction, the promises made by the agent. It is often the most revealing conversation in the whole relationship.

Yet in most companies, these calls are almost never listened to again. A supervisor picks a few each week for quality control. The rest disappear into a recording system nobody looks at.

Emails and tickets are easier to analyze because they are already written. Calls require one more step: transcription. That step has long been the obstacle.

As a result, the company knows the customers who write better than the ones who call, even though callers often have the most urgent or complex problems. An essential part of the voice of the customer remains inaudible to decision-makers.

Transcribe and understand every call

Today's tools can transcribe calls automatically, then analyze them with the same methods as written text. Automatic language analysis identifies reasons for calling, emotions expressed and signs that a customer may leave, across all conversations rather than a sample.

That is what our VoiceIQ module does: call transcription and analysis in five languages, with models such as Mistral, BERT, Llama, GPT or Claude depending on the case. Data stays hosted in France and is never used to train models.

Managers then get an overview of what is said on the phone, week after week.

What companies gain

Analyzing calls tells you why customers really call, and therefore how to reduce avoidable calls by fixing their causes. It also helps spot unhappy customers who will never write a review, but whose voice betrays their frustration.

For a channel that more than half of customers prefer, it is probably one of the most underestimated sources of insight in customer relations.

In practice, a first analysis of one month of calls is often enough to surface three or four avoidable reasons for contact. Fixing them reduces call volume, frees up agent time and improves satisfaction for customers who call about more important matters.

The phone is not a channel of the past. It is an underused one.

What this means for you
